                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Invenergy Transmission LLC                            )       Docket No. EL26-___-000

                   COMPLAINT OF INVENERGY TRANSMISSION LLC

         Pursuant to sections 206, 306, and 309 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 1 and Rule 206

of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

(“Commission” or “FERC”),2 Invenergy Transmission LLC (“Invenergy”) hereby submits this

Complaint against the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”). MISO’s Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”), and MISO’s administration thereof, are unjust,

unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory, because MISO recognizes and actually relies on the

capacity value provided by interregional merchant high-voltage direct current (“HVDC”)

transmission facilities yet refuses to allow those facilities to compete to sell that capacity value.

Invenergy requests that the Commission direct MISO to revise its Tariff to permit interregional

merchant HVDC transmission facilities to be accredited as Capacity Resources.

I.       INTRODUCTION

         Interregional merchant HVDC transmission lines provide real, quantifiable capacity value

to MISO. MISO quantifies that value and actually relies on it to reduce MISO’s region-wide

Planning Reserve Margin (“PRM”). And, because the PRM is lower than it would be without that



1
    16 U.S.C. §§ 824e, 825e, 825h.
2
    18 C.F.R. § 385.206 (2026).
 capacity value, MISO can procure less capacity while still maintaining the same level of reliability,

meaning that MISO’s reliance on that capacity benefits customers throughout the region.

       Nevertheless, although MISO actually relies on that capacity, it refuses to provide any

mechanism for an interregional merchant HVDC transmission line to receive compensation in

exchange. Specifically, MISO’s rules prevent interregional merchant HVDC transmission lines

from being accredited as capacity resources or otherwise receiving compensation for their capacity

value. That means that MISO recognizes the capacity value of an interregional merchant HVDC

facility, relies on the capacity of an interregional merchant HVDC facility, and ensures that the

interregional merchant HVDC facility is not compensated for that service, instead “socializ[ing]”

the benefits across MISO.3

       That refusal is uniquely problematic for merchant transmission lines, which recover their

costs through negotiated rates rather than from captive ratepayers.           Unlike cost-allocated

transmission lines, which elect to receive a return of and return on capital through their

Commission-approved cost-of-service rates rather than payment for each service they provide,

interregional merchant HVDC transmission lines only receive compensation if there is a product

or service—such as capacity—for which they can transact with potential customers. MISO’s

refusal to accredit or otherwise provide a mechanism to compensate interregional merchant HVDC

transmission facilities for the capacity they provide means that there is no product or service that

can be the basis of a merchant-based transaction in MISO.

       That is unjust and unreasonable. MISO’s refusal to accredit or otherwise compensate

interregional merchant HVDC resources for the significant capacity benefits that they provide—

 and on which MISO relies—means that benefits are, necessarily, not being matched with burdens,

as the cost-causation principle requires. 4 That is not an accident, nor is it sufficient to constitute

even the mere “roughly commensurate” matching of costs and benefits that the FPA requires.

Instead, it is an explicit example of one party, in this case, MISO, free-riding completely on the

investments of another, which the FPA’s cost-causation principle prohibits. 5

       It is also unduly discriminatory. MISO treats interregional merchant HVDC transmission

facilities differently from other similarly situated and, indeed, electrically indistinguishable

resources.   Like traditional capacity resources, interregional merchant HVDC transmission

provides capacity value to MISO, which MISO uses to meet its resource adequacy requirements.

That capacity is capable of accreditation by traditional methods and can readily meet MISO’s

performance requirements.      And MISO does not limit accreditation to traditional capacity

resources: it willingly accredits demand response resources, which act less like a traditional

capacity resource than a merchant HVDC facility. Accordingly, refusing to accredit interregional

merchant HVDC resources is undue discrimination.

       The Commission should direct MISO to adopt a replacement rate that allows interregional

merchant HVDC transmission facilities to receive accreditation for the capacity benefits they

provide. Doing so will not entitle them to cost-of-service returns, but will allow the owners of

such facilities to contract with potential offtakers for those capacity benefits that they actually

provide. The most straightforward approach is to build on MISO’s existing resource adequacy

framework by accrediting interregional merchant HVDC using MISO’s Direct Loss of Load

Commission’s duty under the second step of section 206 of the FPA. 6 In the report attached to this

Complaint, Synapse Energy Economics, Inc. (“Synapse”) applies the Direct Loss of Load

Grain Belt Express could provide more than 1,800 MW of accredited capacity under that

methodology.8

       Applying MISO’s accreditation framework to interregional merchant HVDC transmission

is not new. The same logic that allowed MISO to reduce its reserve margin through diversity of

load and resources can be applied to valuing the reliability contributions of interregional merchant

HVDC. To be clear, Invenergy does not seek guaranteed cost recovery for the reliability benefits

that interregional merchant HVDC transmission provides.           Merchant developers of HVDC

transmission take on the risks of development themselves and have no pool of captive customers

from whom to recover costs, by design. But the status quo prevents such a developer from even

competing in the marketplace for compensation for its capacity services. That violates the FPA.

MISO cannot rely on that capacity, to the benefit of other customers, while refusing to provide any

avenue for the entity that provides that capacity to receive commensurate compensation.

 II.      DESCRIPTION OF INVENERGY

         Invenergy and its affiliated companies develop, own, and operate large scale renewable,

energy storage, and thermal generation projects in North America. Invenergy has also developed

over 4,000 miles of transmission and collection lines. Grain Belt Express LLC, a subsidiary of

Invenergy, is currently developing Grain Belt Express, which is planned to be an approximately

800-mile, 5,000 MW HVDC transmission line that will interconnect to the transmission systems

of MISO, Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”), Associated Electric Cooperative Inc., and PJM

Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”). Grain Belt Express will interconnect to the MISO transmission

system pursuant to the Transmission Connection Agreement accepted by the Commission on

February 16, 2024.9 Phase 1 of Grain Belt Express will connect MISO and SPP with 2,500 MW

of transfer capacity beginning in 2031.

III.     BACKGROUND

         A.     Interregional merchant HVDC transmission provides resource adequacy
                value to MISO from specific external generation resources and through
                imports.

         Interregional merchant HVDC transmission facilities support the reliability and

affordability of the bulk power system in several critical respects. One of the most important, and

the subject of this Complaint, is their ability to function similarly to a generation resource by

transmitting, in a fully controllable fashion, electricity from sources on one end of the transmission

line to sinks on the other. That capability can improve resource adequacy in two related, but

distinct ways. First, it can provide firm transmission service to specific generation resources on

the “source” side of the HVDC facility, ensuring that the generation resources’ accredited capacity

can be reliably delivered to the region where it will be counted. 10 MISO describes this benefit as

value of External Resources delivering power via the HVDC transmission facility.

       Second, the transmission capacity on an interregional merchant HVDC transmission

facility that is not needed to deliver a particular generation resource’s accredited capacity also has

independent capacity value. This can be true either if that capacity is unsubscribed or if it is

contracted to a particular generation resource but not needed to deliver that resource’s energy at

all hours, as a resource’s usage is often only a fraction of the resource’s transmission service right

or entitlement.11 MISO describes this benefit as an HVDC transmission facility’s ability to enable

non-firm support. We refer to the aggregate support that a neighboring system can provide,

separate from specific External Resources that participate directly in MISO’s capacity market, as

“external pooled capacity.” We refer to the HVDC transmission facility’s ability to enable this

capacity as the capacity value of the HVDC transmission facility itself.

       Both forms of capacity value are well recognized. MISO “understands and acknowledges

that the new HVDC-enabled resources can contribute to reliability and resource adequacy of the

MISO system.”12 MISO has explained that “HVDC transmission today can enable Firm External

Resources to participate in the MISO [Planning Resource Auction] for capacity credit and can

additionally provide non-firm support contributing to overall reliability.” 13 For that reason, MISO

incorporates firm and non-firm support that it reasonably expects to meet electricity demand,

taking into account transmission constraints and excess available energy that external areas can

offer MISO, into its resource adequacy modeling.14 And MISO has recognized that there are

        The Commission also has recognized the reliability benefits from interregional HVDC

        B.      MISO relies on the full resource adequacy value of interregional HVDC
                transmission.

        MISO does not just recognize the resource adequacy value of an interregional HVDC

transmission line: it actually relies on both components of that value, the capacity of specific

External Resources delivered by HVDC transmission and the capacity of the HVDC transmission

itself. With regard to the former, specific generation resources on the “source” side of a

transmission facility can participate in MISO’s capacity construct as Capacity Resources and are

       C.      Although MISO recognizes and relies on resource adequacy contributions
               from interregional HVDC transmission facilities, it refuses to give merchant
               facilities an opportunity to receive compensation for their contributions.

       But while MISO relies on the capacity of interregional HVDC transmission facilities, it

refuses to accredit that capacity, which would provide a path for merchant interregional HVDC

Instead of providing that path, MISO, in its own words, “socialize[s]” that capacity value, 35 which

means that it relies on the capacity enabled by interregional HVDC transmission to reduce other

entities’ capacity obligations, without compensating merchant facilities for that benefit.

       To date, MISO has articulated two reasons for that refusal. First, accrediting HVDC “could

be complicated,” requiring changes in modeling and coordination and a new process to “separate

the reliability benefits provided by transmission lines from the reliability benefits provided by

generators using the transmission lines.”36 Second, accrediting HVDC “cannot be isolated from a

holistic assessment of overall HVDC integration”37 (though MISO will not articulate when that

holistic assessment will take place).38

IV.    COMPLAINT

       A.      MISO’s failure to accredit the capacity value of interregional merchant HVDC
               transmission is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory.

               1.      MISO’s Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it does not allow
                       interregional merchant HVDC transmission facilities to compete for or
                       receive compensation for the resource adequacy benefits that they
                       provide and on which MISO actually relies.

       Interregional merchant HVDC transmission provides MISO with unequivocal resource

adequacy and reliability benefits. That includes both the capacity value of specific External

Resources connected to MISO by an HVDC transmission facility and the capacity value of an

HVDC transmission facility itself. And, as described above, MISO actually relies on both forms

of resource adequacy contribution: it relies on the capacity of the HVDC facility to reduce the

PRM, and it relies on HVDC-enabled External Resources as Capacity Resources to satisfy that

value.39 Instead, those benefits are “socialized,” which MISO apparently understands to mean

       That is unjust and unreasonable. Courts and the Commission have “[f]or decades”

understood the “just and reasonable” statutory standard to incorporate a “cost-causation”

principle,41 which requires that costs be allocated to beneficiaries in a manner at least roughly

commensurate with benefits.42 In this way, the cost-causation principle “manifests a kind of

equity”43 by requiring the Commission to ensure that “burden is matched with benefit” 44 such that

“a few customers” do not “pay the entire cost of a facility that benefits many.” 45

        The practical effect of the cost-causation principle has been described by the courts as an

imperative to combat “free-ridership”—the phenomenon in which one or more entities realize

benefits from investments paid for predominantly or even entirely by other customers. 46 Although

the cost-causation principle does not establish an absolute prohibition on any free-ridership

whatsoever—after all, benefits need only be “roughly commensurate” with burdens 47—the courts

have set aside Commission orders that would have incorporated the potential for free-ridership and

subsidization as features of the relevant tariff, rather than as unintentional consequences of the

messy exercise that is the identification and assignment of the benefits of energy infrastructure. 48

       The cost-causation principle is an instantiation of the just and reasonable standard 49 and,

therefore, applies to all aspects of rates and practices subject to the Commission’s jurisdiction

under sections 205 and 206 of the FPA—not just to transmission facilities that recover their costs

from captive customers. The Commission has been clear that it has the authority and responsibility

to ensure that cost allocation of merchant developers’ investments complies with the cost-

causation principle. For example, the Commission’s interconnection pricing policy allocates

network upgrade costs—triggered by the interconnection of particular generating facilities,

including merchant generating facilities—into embedded cost rates paid by load. 50 In National

     II.   RESOURCE ADEQUACY BENEFITS OF INTERREGIONAL HVDC
           TRANSMISSION

 1   Q7.   Please explain how interregional HVDC transmission enables the flow of energy

 2         between operating regions.

 3   A7.   HVDC facilities are capable of efficiently transferring energy over long distances

 4         between different operating regions. Because HVDC facilities are fully controllable

 5         and dispatchable (unlike traditional transmission facilities), operators can direct power

 6         flows precisely when and where they are needed most during reliability events. They

 7         are also valuable for connecting regions with complementary resource and demand

 8         profiles, as load patterns, generation availability, and weather conditions vary across

 9         regions.

10   Q8.   Please elaborate on how interregional HVDC transmission can deliver capacity

11         across operating regions, including from both (i) specific external generating

12         resources and (ii) the capacity value of the transmission facility itself.

13   A8.   Interregional HVDC transmission facilities improve resource adequacy through two

14         means. First, HVDC transmission facilities can enable the capacity market participation

15         of individual external resources located outside of MISO. These resources would be

16         unable to connect across operating regions without dispatchable HVDC technology.

17         Additionally, interregional HVDC transmission improves access to aggregate excess

18         energy from resources in neighboring regions. For purposes of my testimony, I refer to

19         the aggregate support that a neighboring system can provide, separate from specific

20         external resources that participate directly in MISO’s capacity market, as “external
                                                                                             Docket No. EL26-___-000
                                                                                                        Attachment A
                                                                                                         Page 4 of 19

 1            pooled capacity.” Energy from external pooled capacity is especially likely to flow into

 2            MISO during critical periods due to high energy prices caused by system stress.

 3   Q9.      How have energy flows from neighboring regions supported MISO in recent

 4            critical events?

 5   A9.      As I discussed in the Synapse Report, MISO has repeatedly imported energy from its

 6            neighbors during periods of system stress to maintain reliability during extreme events.

 7            For example, during a recent heatwave in July 2026, MISO imported over 15 GW from

 8            neighboring regions during peak hours, with nearly 3.6 GW of energy coming from

 9            SPP.1 Furthermore, the quantity of flows during these critical periods is often far greater

10            than the average energy imports throughout the rest of the year, due to higher energy

11            pricing. This indicates that MISO’s current approach to modeling interregional

12            connections, which relies on average flows throughout the year, is insufficient for

13            capturing their reliability contributions during critical periods, as I discuss further in

14            A10 below.

16            transmission in setting its Planning Reserve Margin?

     IV.       ACCREDITATION OF INTERREGIONAL HVDC TRANSMISSION
               CAPACITY

 8   Q11. What is MISO’s DLOL-based capacity accreditation framework?

 9   A11.      MISO’s DLOL-based resource accreditation methodology seeks to quantify the

10             availability of resources during peak stress conditions, and it reflects the fraction of a

11             resource’s nameplate capacity that can be used to fulfill reserve margin requirements.4

12             When the methodology takes effect in the 2028-2029 planning year, MISO will accredit

13             all resource classes with the DLOL-based method.5 The DLOL methodology measures

14             resource availability during the tightest risk hours using a probabilistic model. MISO’s

15             model covers 30 historical years of hourly weather patterns, five load-forecast

16             uncertainty bands, and 50 random outage draws, resulting in 7,500 year-long hourly

17             simulations of MISO’s system.6 Once the model is calibrated to MISO’s target 0.1 loss

18             of load expectation (LOLE) metric, MISO uses outputs from this simulation to identify

19             the riskiest hours, otherwise known as Critical Hours, which are defined as hours that

 2            then ranks the Critical Hours by risk and weights them so that hours with higher risk

 3            count more heavily toward the DLOL calculation. Finally, for each season, the DLOL-

 4            based accreditation is calculated as the weighted average availability of all resources

 5            within the resource class, across all Critical Hours.8

 7            apply to interregional HVDC transmission?

 8   A12.     Yes. Our analysis detailed in the Synapse Report demonstrated the feasibility of

 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Electric utilities, grid operators, and regulators across the country are grappling with a fundamental
challenge: maintaining a system that is both reliable and affordable for customers in the face of
unprecedented demands. Rapid load growth combined with supply chain constraints and restrictive
local permitting processes call for unique solutions to maintain resource adequacy without placing an
unsustainable cost burden on customers.

Interregional high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission          Figure 1. Proposed GBX transmission
facilities can make significant contributions to supporting            line
                                                                       Map of GBX transmission line
resource adequacy by enabling the flow of energy between
different operating regions. When energy is most needed, during
periods of system stress, HVDC enables energy transfers from
other regions with excess energy. System stress events often
occur at different times in different regions, as load patterns,
generation availability, and weather conditions vary across
regions. HVDC facilities can efficiently move large amounts of
energy over long distances and connect regions with
complementary resource and demand profiles.

Importantly, because merchant-owned HVDC transmission
facilities cannot access the same rate-base financing mechanisms
used by utility-owned projects, merchant-owned interregional
HVDC transmission facilities require functioning markets to
incentivize project investments. To enable participation and compensation within wholesale markets,
those markets must assign value to the benefits brought by HVDC transmission facilities. Within the
Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) system specifically, accreditation of interregional
HVDC facilities can create an investment signal for development of this technology.

In this analysis, we develop a case study, based on Phase 1 of the Grain Belt Express (GBX) HVDC
transmission line, to demonstrate how MISO could apply its direct loss of load (DLOL)-based
accreditation methodology to HVDC facilities. Phase 1 of GBX is planned to connect MISO and SPP with
2,500 MW transfer capacity beginning in 2031 (see location in MISO and SPP in Figure 1). Using the
modeling tool MISO uses for resource accreditation, we simultaneously model both SPP and MISO to
produce a detailed, hourly simulation of the availability of energy from SPP into MISO. MISO’s DLOL-
based accreditation calculation measures resource availability during the riskiest modeled hours in the
simulation. Similarly, we measure SPP’s available energy into MISO through the GBX transmission link

Electric utilities, grid operators, and regulators require new solutions to maintain a system that is both
reliable and affordable in the face of unprecedented demands. Load growth combined with supply chain
constraints, backlogged interconnection queues, and increasingly restrictive local permitting processes
are culminating in substantial concerns about how to maintain resource adequacy without placing an
unsustainable cost burden on customers.

Interregional high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission facilities can make unique and significant
contributions to supporting resource adequacy by enabling the flow of energy between different
operating regions. Because load patterns, generation availability, and weather conditions vary across
regions, system stress events often occur at different times and in different locations. HVDC facilities can
efficiently move large amounts of energy over long distances and connect regions with complementary
resource and demand profiles. Unlike traditional transmission facilities, HVDC facilities are fully
controllable and dispatchable, allowing operators to direct power flows precisely when and where they
are most needed during reliability events.

The Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s (MISO) past experience demonstrates the value of
access to external resources during periods of system stress. For example, during a recent heatwave in
July 2026, MISO imported over 15 GW from neighboring regions during peak hours, with nearly 3.6 GW
of energy coming from the Southwest Power Pool (SPP).1 During Winter Storm Uri in 2021, MISO
imported up to 13 GW of energy from the PJM Interconnection (PJM) regional system to the east.2
During Winter Storms Heather and Fern, MISO imported approximately 7.5 GW from PJM.3 Time and
time again, interregional connections have proved invaluable in helping MISO maintain reliability during
extreme events. Furthermore, the quantity of flows during these critical periods is often far greater than
the average energy imports throughout the rest of the year due to higher energy pricing. This indicates
that MISO’s current approach to modeling interregional connections, which relies on average flows
throughout the year, is insufficient for capturing their reliability contributions during critical periods.

In this report, we focus on explaining and quantifying the reliability contributions of interregional
merchant HVDC transmission facilities specifically. While strengthening traditional alternating current
(AC) transmission connections can also offer reliability benefits, the dispatchable nature of HVDC
transmission facilities enables them to provide more precise and controllable resource adequacy
contributions. Furthermore, the investment signal for transmission facilities developed by incumbent

In MISO’s reserve margin calculation, the external pooled capacity reduces the amount of total firm
capacity needed to maintain MISO’s acceptable level of risk.6 As a result, the more external pooled
capacity present in the reserve margin study, the lower the reserve margin requirement result will be
across the MISO system for all load-serving entities. Therefore, while MISO currently acknowledges the

compensated for this benefit. As such, there is currently no market signal in MISO’s capacity market, or

characteristics that reflect hourly availability, it models pooled external support less carefully. MISO
currently models external pooled capacity in its reserve margin study as a single generator with a
random, probabilistic distribution of available capacity, reflecting an average of the last five years of
energy imports.7 The result is a less accurate representation in which MISO shows external pooled
capacity as a single source and aggregates availability across all transmission lines.

 2.1.     Methodology and input assumptions
We keep our methods and data assumptions as consistent as possible with MISO’s DLOL methodology.
We only make adjustments where necessary to accurately model interregional transmission.

Input assumption data
We rely on PowerGEM’s Eastern Interconnection database as a foundation for building our model. The
Eastern Interconnection database includes unit-level resource representations, as well as historical
hourly data on wind, solar, and load profiles. We then layer on changes to the load and resource supply
to develop projections for 2031. Our load and resource supply assumptions are based on forecasts from
each of the two RTOs. For MISO, our projections are based on data from its Futures study, specifically
the Future 2, Series 2 scenario.21 For SPP, our projections are based on its 2025 FERNS study.22

As with any technology, GBX’s DLOL accreditation value will depend on the load and resource portfolio
assumptions. If the future resource portfolio and loads vary significantly from the RTOs’ current
forecasts, the DLOL accreditation value may change.

Appendix A: Modeling Assumptions contains more detail on our modeling assumptions, including for
load, resources, and topology.

Methods
As with MISO’s studies, we rely on the SERVM probabilistic modeling tool to estimate resource
accreditation. Like MISO, we use 30 weather years of historical data, the same peak load-level
uncertainty distribution, and 50 iterations. Also like MISO’s Planning Reserve Margin Requirement study,
we model MISO as a “copper plate” model, meaning there are no transmission constraints between
zones and energy can flow freely among all 10 zones.

Unlike in MISO’s studies, we model the SPP system at the resource level and add transmission
connections between the two regions. We model existing transmission connections between MISO and
SPP, as well as the proposed GBX line. Therefore, the availability of energy from SPP in our model is
based on a detailed representation of projected load and unit-level resource deployment in that RTO, as
opposed to the random availability draw that MISO’s studies use. This produces a much more accurate
representation of external support that will be available to MISO.

In this case study we adapt MISO’s study model so that some resources are dispatched economically. In
MISO’s studies, all resources are modeled using SERVM’s “must-run” settings, meaning they operate at
their maximum possible output, regardless of unit economics. This is because MISO’s DLOL method is
intended to capture a resource’s availability, not its economic competitiveness during high-risk hours.

that we do not include outage assumptions on the transmission lines.

or removing flat load.23 Per MISO’s methodology, we adjust the flat load until the system reaches an
annual 0.1 LOLE. Next, we further adjust the seasons with less than 0.01 LOLE, until the season reaches
0.01 LOLE. We simultaneously calibrate SPP’s system to 0.1 annual LOLE, by following SPP’s method of
adding positive or negative flat load until winter and summer both reach 0.05 LOLE.24

3.2.     Benefits of accrediting GBX on the supply side, as opposed to the current

MISO’s current process for modeling external pooled capacity in its reserve margin calculation fails to
accurately capture its true resource adequacy benefit, which we discuss in Section 1.2. Since the
availability of external pooled capacity is randomly selected in MISO’s model based on historical data for
energy flows in all hours, as opposed to the actual unit characteristics behind the external pooled
capacity, it is not an accurate representation of the external pooled capacity availability during MISO’s
critical periods, and it is likely underestimating the availability of external pooled capacity.

MISO’s model draws from a normally distributed random distribution of external support, which is
centered around average availability in all hours. Therefore, the randomly selected availability during
critical hours in MISO’s modeling is likely to be around the average of the distribution and reflect
average flows during all hours, as opposed to the elevated flows that are likely to occur during high
priced, critical hours.32 Since our DLOL-based analysis indicates the availability of GBX during critical
hours is greater than the average availability of external support included in MISO’s model, our method
would result in a higher level of external pooled capacity in MISO’s capacity market modeling.33

MISO’s modeling approach will reduce the reserve margin requirement used to develop the demand
curve. However, there is a lack of transparency around the reserve margin impacts of external support in
MISO’s modeling. MISO does not publish the amount of pooled external capacity included in its reserve
margin requirement calculation. Further, MISO does not publish enough information or data to
independently recreate this method in SERVM. Therefore, the precise magnitude of the difference in

 4.       CONCLUSION
In this analysis, we demonstrate the resource adequacy benefit of interregional HVDC facilities using the
same methods and modeling tools that MISO uses for DLOL-based accreditation. We recognize that this
analysis would require MISO to make changes to its current modeling methods. Most significantly,
MISO’s model would require a unit-level representation of SPP’s system, using the same modeling that
MISO currently uses for its internal system. This may require some level of coordination with SPP to
ensure that its system is represented correctly. However, this would unlock significant benefits through
a much more accurate representation of SPP’s surplus capacity availability during the highest-risk hours
in MISO’s study.

We also demonstrate the significant ratepayer cost benefits of accrediting HVDC facilities. Merchant-
owned HVDC transmission facilities do not have the same rate-base financing mechanisms available that
utility-owned alternating current transmission projects do. As such, interregional HVDC transmission
facilities require valuation of their benefits to participate in wholesale markets. Accreditation of
interregional HVDC facilities in MISO would create an investment signal for development of such
technology. As we present in Section 3.1, MISO’s North/Central region would have seen $1.8 billion in
cost savings with the addition of GBX in the 2026/27 PRA.

By using the same analytical tools and methods MISO uses, we also demonstrate the feasibility for MISO
to include this accreditation analysis in the annual study cycle. We have shown through our modeling
methods description in Section 2.1 that SERVM can be configured to produce the incremental capacity
that a new transmission line brings to MISO’s system during highest-risk hours. We also demonstrate
that SERVM can be configured to produce the outputs required for the DLOL-based accreditation
calculation.

Many of the modeling adjustments we made to MISO’s current methods are within the SERVM tool
itself. We anticipate that the most significant effort for MISO to adopt this analysis would be the
inclusion of SPP, and potentially other neighboring areas as HVDC development expands. Given the
benefits this analysis brings to MISO and its members, we believe it is worth MISO’s effort to include
detailed representation of neighboring regions in its study model.

Finally, we acknowledge MISO’s many planned efforts to improve its study modeling in the future,
including better representation of transmission, both within MISO and with other regions.34 The DLOL-
based accreditation method, and thus MISO’s reserve requirement calculation, is highly sensitive to the
model’s inputs and assumptions. Coupled with the modeling in SERVM to build the market’s reliability-
based demand curve, MISO’s calculation for the auction clearing price relies heavily on the SERVM
model. As such, MISO’s study model requires continuous improvement as system conditions evolve. In
this case study, we demonstrate the benefits and feasibility of one such model improvement.

     II.   THE CURRENT ROLE OF HVDC TRANSMISSION IN MISO’S RESOURCE
           ADEQUACY CONSTRUCT

 1   Q7.   How do the actions of MISO, states, load-serving entities, and generation

 2         developers together ensure resource adequacy in the MISO region?

 3   A7.   Resource adequacy in MISO is a shared undertaking among participants performing

 4         different functions. States and other Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authorities

 5         retain authority over resource adequacy matters within their jurisdiction, including

 6         oversight of the load-serving entities that plan for and secure capacity for their

 7         customers. MISO’s Tariff is designed to complement, rather than displace, that state

 8         authority.

 9         MISO provides the regional analytical and market framework. Each year, MISO

10         performs a probabilistic LOLE study and establishes a Planning Reserve Margin for

11         each season. The study evaluates the amount of unforced capacity needed above

12         forecast coincident peak demand to satisfy MISO’s reliability criterion. MISO then

13         uses the applicable Planning Reserve Margin, the load forecasts submitted for each

14         load-serving entity, and transmission-loss adjustments to calculate each load-serving

15         entity’s seasonal Planning Reserve Margin Requirement. MISO also establishes Local

16         Reliability Requirements and transmission-based import and export limits so that

17         regional capacity is not treated as deliverable without regard to locational constraints.

18         Each load-serving entity is responsible for demonstrating that it can satisfy its seasonal

19         requirement. Under MISO’s construct, a load-serving entity may designate Zonal

20         Resource Credits through a Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan, self-schedule credits,

21         purchase credits through the Planning Resource Auction, or address a deficiency
                                                                          Docket No. EL26-___-000
                                                                                Attachment No. B
                                                                                     Page 4 of 13

 1         through the Tariff’s deficiency mechanism. The Planning Resource Auction is

 2         conducted annually but clears separately by season and location, respecting Local

 3         Clearing Requirements and Capacity Import and Export Limits. Resources whose

 4         capacity is used to satisfy an obligation are subject to the applicable qualification,

 5         accreditation, offer, and performance requirements.

 6         Developers and resource owners respond to the resulting planning requirements,

 7         bilateral contracting opportunities, and market prices. Those signals influence

 8         decisions to retain, retire, or add generation and other qualifying resources.

 9         Together, state and load-serving entity planning decisions establish the underlying

10         needs, MISO translates those needs into regional and locational requirements and

11         administers the compliance framework, and developers invest in resources that may be

12         used to meet those requirements.

13   Q8.   Does the current design of the MISO resource adequacy construct incentivize the

14         development of new merchant HVDC transmission connecting MISO with other

15         regions?

16   A8.   No. MISO recognizes the reliability benefit of external support in its resource adequacy

17         analysis, but the construct does not presently provide a general capacity accreditation

18         pathway for the uncontracted transfer capability of a merchant interregional HVDC

19         facility. As a result, merchant interregional HVDC facilities contribute to the reliability

20         outcome reflected in the LOLE study without receiving a corresponding quantity of

21         accredited capacity that can be converted into Zonal Resource Credits and monetized

22         through bilateral transactions, a Fixed Resource Adequacy Plan, or the Planning

23         Resource Auction.

 1   That point is reflected in the distinction between firm and non-firm imports in MISO’s

 2   LOLE study. Firm external resources are modeled at the individual resource level using

 3   their installed or contracted capacity and seasonal outage assumptions. By contrast,

 4   non-firm external support is modeled as a seasonal probability distribution derived

 5   from historical net scheduled interchange after subtracting firm imports and off-system

 6   exports. In each simulated hour, the model uses a random draw to represent the external

 7   capacity that may be available to MISO. That probabilistic support reduces modeled

 8   system risk and therefore can reduce the amount of additional unforced capacity

 9   required to achieve the LOLE criterion.

10   This treatment recognizes system-level reliability value, but it does not assign that

11   value to the owner of the transmission capability that enables the imports. Cost-of-

12   service transmission generally has a regulated opportunity to recover its costs and an

13   authorized return from customers. A merchant line instead depends on negotiated

14   revenues. If its resource adequacy contribution lowers requirements for load but cannot

15   be separately accredited and sold, that contribution is not directly monetizable by the

16   merchant developer. In my view, that asymmetry weakens the investment signal for

17   merchant interregional transmission and can result in less development than would

18   occur if the resource adequacy value were attributed to the facility that provides it.

     III.   ACCREDITATION OF INTERREGIONAL HVDC TRANSMISSION
            CAPACITY

 1   Q9.    What changes to MISO’s resource adequacy systems and processes would be

 2          required for MISO to implement capacity accreditation for interregional HVDC

 3          transmission lines?

 4   A9.    First, MISO would need a methodology to identify the reliable seasonal capacity

 5          contribution of an eligible HVDC transmission facility. The methodology would

 6          recognize the portion of the facility’s capacity contribution associated with a firm

 7          external resource or other capacity arrangement, if any. The methodology also would

 8          include rules to clearly allocate accredited capacity between the transmission facility

 9          and external resources using the facility so that the same transfer capability is not

10          credited twice. In other words, MISO would need a framework to determine how much

11          accredited capacity is assigned to rights holders of the HVDC facility itself versus how

12          much is assigned to external resources receiving firm transmission service over the line.

13          The report by Synapse Energy Economics, Inc. (Synapse) included in Attachment A to

14          this Complaint provides an example of a workable approach. It demonstrates how

15          MISO could first recognize the accredited value of contracted external resources, with

16          the remaining transfer capability available for accreditation as the transmission

17          facility’s incremental reliability contribution, thereby avoiding double counting of

18          transfers over the HVDC transmission facility while preserving recognition of both

19          sources of resource adequacy value.

20          For uncontracted capability, the methodology would need to quantify the incremental

21          reliability contribution of the controllable transfer capability, taking account of the
                                                                   Docket No. EL26-___-000
                                                                         Attachment No. B
                                                                              Page 7 of 13

 1   availability of the line, the availability of external supply, operating restrictions, and

 2   conditions during the hours in which MISO experiences loss-of-load risk. Synapse’s

 3   report also provides a workable framework for this approach. Additional details would

 4   require further elaboration.

 5   Second, MISO would need an explicit accounting adjustment to prevent double

 6   counting of imports that reduce the regional Planning Reserve Margin and the HVDC

 7   transmission facility’s accredited capacity. To the extent accredited HVDC capacity is

 8   carved out and treated as a discrete Planning Resource or capacity product, the same

 9   megawatts should not remain in the historical non-firm-support distribution that

10   reduces the system Planning Reserve Margin. MISO would therefore need to remove

11   the accredited contribution from the non-firm import data or otherwise adjust the LOLE

12   model so that the facility’s value is counted once: either as accredited capacity or as

13   undifferentiated probabilistic external support, but not both.

14   Third, MISO would need qualification, registration, deliverability, and performance

15   rules. Those rules should identify who may register the capability, what transmission

16   rights and external supply arrangements must be demonstrated, how outages and

17   derates are reported, how seasonal accreditation is converted into Zonal Resource

18   Credits, and what offer or availability obligations apply when the accredited capability

19   is committed to serve MISO load. The rules also should address imports during

20   emergencies, coordination with neighboring systems, and consequences for non-

23   tracking, auction, settlement, and compliance systems and document the resulting

 5   Q10. You highlight the need to develop accounting mechanisms to avoid double

 6          counting. Can you explain what “double counting” means in this context and why

 7          this is a concern?

 8   A10.   There are two forms of potential double counting that MISO would need to address.

 9          First, MISO would need to prevent double counting between an interregional HVDC

10          facility and external resources using the facility. For example, if a portion of the line’s

11          transfer capability is already committed to deliver capacity from a specific external

12          resource registered separately into MISO, that same capability should not also be

13          accredited as incremental capacity provided by the transmission facility itself. MISO

14          would need rules to allocate accredited capacity between the transmission facility and

15          separate external resources receiving transmission service over the facility. As

16          discussed above, the Synapse report included with this filing demonstrates one

17          potential approach by recognizing the accredited contribution of contracted external

18          resources and then evaluating any remaining transfer capability separately, thus

19          avoiding duplicative accreditation of the same capability.

20          Second, MISO would need to prevent double counting between accredited HVDC

21          capacity and the external support that MISO already accounts for in its resource

22          adequacy framework. Today, MISO’s LOLE studies recognize the probabilistic

23          contribution of external generation that may be available to support MISO during
                                                                           Docket No. EL26-___-000
                                                                                 Attachment No. B
                                                                                      Page 9 of 13

 1          periods of system stress. If MISO were to separately accredit the reliability value of an

 2          interregional HVDC facility, that value should not remain embedded within the

 3          external support assumptions used to calculate Planning Reserve Margin

 4          Requirements. Otherwise, the same reliability contribution could be recognized twice:

 5          once through accredited capacity and again through the external support reflected in

 6          MISO’s LOLE modeling. Accounting adjustments would be needed so that the

 7          reliability value is counted once within the construct.

 8   Q11. If MISO were to accredit interregional HVDC based on the external pooled

 9          capacity, MISO would not have operational control over the external resources

10          delivering energy on the interregional HVDC line. Do you view this as a barrier

11          to accrediting interregional HVDC?

12   A11.   No. While MISO would not have operational control over many of the external

13          resources contributing to the reliability value of the interregional HVDC facility, that

14          fact is not unique to HVDC accreditation. MISO already treats external resources that

15          are not pseudo-tied into MISO and are therefore not under MISO’s direct operational

16          control as Planning Resources. MISO’s FERC-approved framework recognizes that

17          these resources can contribute to reliability, even though their availability is subject to

18          transmission conditions, market incentives, and the actions of neighboring balancing

19          authorities.

20          Similarly, accreditation of an interregional HVDC facility would not require MISO to

21          exercise operational control over each individual external resource contributing to the

22          HVDC facility’s reliability value. Instead, the methodology would estimate the

23          expected contribution to reliability based on historical performance, transmission
                                                                          Docket No. EL26-___-000
                                                                                Attachment No. B
                                                                                     Page 10 of 13

 1          availability, external supply availability, and system conditions during periods of loss

 2          of load and/or risk. This is a risk-based assessment, like other accreditation methods

 3          used by MISO.

 4          Further, all Market Participants receiving accreditation face significant financial

 5          incentives to ensure their capacity is available when needed, including the risk of

 6          capacity replacement obligations, market purchases, and other non-performance

 7          penalties.

 8   Q12. In sum, based on your experience, do you believe that MISO can practically

 9          implement the changes required to accredit the capacity value of HVDC

10          transmission?

11   A12.   Yes. In my experience administering MISO’s resource adequacy construct, the required

12          work is institutionally feasible. MISO already conducts an annual probabilistic LOLE

13          study, models firm external resources and probabilistic non-firm support, determines

14          seasonal import and export limits, qualifies multiple types of Planning Resources,

15          converts Seasonal Accredited Capacity into Zonal Resource Credits, and administers

16          seasonal auction and performance requirements. Accreditation of eligible HVDC

17          capability would require a new methodology and associated Tariff and system changes,

18          but it would use those existing institutional building blocks.

19          The principal challenges are defining the accredited product, demonstrating that

20          external supply can be delivered over the facility during risk hours, allocating value

21          between contracted and uncontracted portions, coordinating outages and operating

22          requirements, and preventing double counting in the LOLE study and capacity market.

                                  NOTICE OF COMPLAINT
         Take notice that on November 4, 2026, Invenergy Transmission LLC filed a formal
complaint against Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), pursuant to
Sections 206, 306, and 309 of the Federal Power Act and Rule 206 of the Commission’s Rules of
Practice and Procedure, alleging that MISO’s tariff, and MISO’s administration thereof, are
unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory, because MISO recognizes and actually relies on
the capacity value provided by interregional merchant high-voltage direct current transmission
facilities yet refuses to allow those facilities to compete to sell that capacity value.

        Invenergy certifies that copies of the complaint were served on the contacts for MISO as
listed on the Commission’s list of Corporate Officials.

be taken but will not serve to make protestants parties to the proceeding. Any person wishing to
become a party must file a notice of intervention or motion to intervene, as appropriate. The
Respondent’s answer and all interventions, or protests must be filed on or before the comment
date. The Respondent’s answer, motions to intervene, and protests must be served on Invenergy.
